source.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Charles O'Neill; Christine Ye; Kartheik Iyer; John F. Wu

page_placements.theme: Feature families, containment and co-activation modules within a single SAE

record.tranche_reason: Measures decoder-vector similarities and feature relationships across SAE capacities, and analyzes feature families, using dense text embeddings rather than the original transformer-activation setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on nearest-neighbour alignment across SAE sizes, examples of splitting and novel features, consistency of matches across sizes, and within-SAE feature-family structure. Cited results from other work and semantic-search intervention results are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: Trains top-k SAEs of several sizes on dense text embeddings (text-embedding-3-small, arXiv abstracts). It compares decoder directions across SAE sizes and reports splitting, recurrent and novel features. This is a new setting with its own results on V1, V3 and V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors find both recurrent and novel features across sizes, and nearest-neighbour similarity falls with k and n, which they read as finer features. Splitting is clean in some examples (periodicity) but not others (LBV), and cross-size matches are not self-consistent. They also say smaller SAEs may not cover the feature space. Feature families are a separate, within-SAE co-activation hierarchy.
record.recipe_differences: Top-k SAEs trained on normalized text embeddings; feature comparison uses decoder-vector nearest neighbours, activation similarity, and graph-based within-SAE families rather than a transformer-activation SAE split analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Nearest-neighbour similarity decreases as k and n increase; recurrence is more common at lower k. Family activation-similarity ratios differ by dataset and SAE capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: Within a single SAE, co-activation-defined families have a dense parent and sparse children. Median parent-child co-occurrence ratios are 1.22–11.75. Activation-similarity block ratios are 0.89–5.87 and are weak for cs.LG SAE16/SAE32.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within one SAE, features form parent–child co-activation hierarchies, independent of dictionary-size splitting.

record.problems: Feature-splitting examples are partly qualitative; nearest-neighbour distributions are presented in figures without textual numeric values. The reported comparisons do not directly establish that larger features partition smaller-feature inputs. Feature-family metrics are medians, and some cs.LG activation-similarity ratios show little or no in-block advantage.

untested.parts: Whether finer features partition or cover the parent's inputs is not quantified.
All of it: no LLM-internal activations, no open SAE releases, and no other SAE families. Only the authors' top-k SAEs on output text embeddings.
Whether split features mirror a concept hierarchy in the model's representation. The within-SAE families are a different construct.
Whether larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents.

missing.what: No meaningful block-diagonal structure or clustering is found in decoder matrix W. This bears on the geometric closeness of feature groups.
PCA projections show families are linear subspaces, not manifolds.

record.verdict_notes: V2 was dropped: SAEs on an API embedding model's outputs differ from SAEs on model-internal activations or open SAE releases. Tranche set to T3 (new setting) rather than T2. The cross-size evidence is mostly qualitative single examples plus figure-only distributions. Appendix E.1 contradicts itself on whether recurrence rises or falls with k; the main text says recurrence is more common at lower k.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly quantify whether the inputs activating a smaller feature are partitioned among its larger-SAE matches.
Tests SAEs on embeddings from OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and its own released SAEs, not large language model internal activations or other open SAE releases.
Studies hierarchical families within individual SAEs, but does not establish that cross-size split features form nested families mirroring a concept hierarchy.
Absorption and parent-child takeover are not measured.
Reports novel larger-SAE features and cross-size alignment, but does not test whether larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents.
Does not compare sparsity objectives or test whether the splitting pattern is an artifact of the training objective.

rows.subject: SAE pairs across astro-ph and cs.LG
rows.size_stated: SAE16, SAE32, SAE64; n varies across 3072, 6144, and 9216 in the plotted comparisons
rows.operation_detail: Compared nearest-neighbour decoder-vector cosine similarity across SAE sizes while varying n at fixed k; distributions combine astro-ph and cs.LG.
rows.measure: Distribution of maximum nearest-neighbour cosine similarity
rows.value: figure only; text says increasing n reduces nearest-neighbour similarity
rows.note: The text interprets lower similarity at higher capacity as greater differentiation; numerical distribution values are not given.
rows.check: Figure-only distributions with no numbers. Lower nearest-neighbour cosine does not show whether finer features cover a parent's inputs. Dropped V2: SAEs on output embeddings are not LLM-internal activations or open SAE families.

rows.subject: astro-ph SAEs: SAE16, SAE32, SAE64
rows.operation_detail: Compared feature directions and semantic interpretations for the periodicity feature across SAE sizes.
rows.measure: Qualitative cross-size feature splitting and pairwise cosine similarity
rows.value: Authors describe a top-level periodicity feature across all three SAEs, with increasing numbers of more granular features; figure only for cosine values.
rows.note: The authors call this an example of canonical splitting, but do not report a quantitative partition of the parent feature's inputs.
rows.check: Authors call it canonical splitting: a universal periodicity feature with more granular features at larger sizes. Qualitative, single example. Dropped V2 and V3; this is cross-size splitting, not a tested hierarchy.

rows.subject: astro-ph SAEs: SAE16, SAE32, SAE64
rows.operation_detail: Examined nearest-neighbour features associated with the Luminous Blue Variables feature across SAE sizes.
rows.value: SAE64 has additional nearest-neighbour features labelled LTB Models and Lyman Break Galaxies; the authors say these are highly dissimilar and unrelated to the LBV feature and to features in smaller SAEs.
rows.note: The authors suggest this grouping could be a spurious acronym-level correlation, rather than meaningful semantic splitting.
rows.check: For the LBV feature, SAE64's extra nearest neighbours are unrelated, so there is no semantic splitting. The novel-feature aspect for V5 is already captured in r8, so V3 and V5 were removed here.

rows.subject: astro-ph SAEs: SAE16, SAE32, SAE64
rows.operation_detail: Compared decoder-vector cosine and activation similarity for a recurrent feature across SAE sizes.
rows.measure: Feature-vector cosine similarity and activation similarity
rows.value: All feature-vector cosine similarities are >0.98; the feature occurs as one feature in each model.
rows.note: Shows a highly aligned feature recurring across sizes, rather than a split.
rows.check: The O-type stars feature recurs as a single feature at every size (cosine >0.98) and does not split. This is a counterexample, not a partial effect.

rows.subject: SAEs with n=3072, 6144, and 9216
rows.operation_detail: Counted features from the smallest SAE with highly aligned features in the larger SAEs.
rows.value: Over 1100 triplets for k=16; the number drops sharply as k increases.
rows.note: The count demonstrates recurrent directions, but does not show that larger features partition smaller-feature inputs.
rows.check: The count of recurrent triplets does not test splitting. The appendix contradicts itself: it says 'more features re-occur for higher k', then reports a sharp drop as k rises. Removed V5.

rows.subject: SAE16, SAE32, SAE64
rows.operation_detail: Compared direct SAE16-to-SAE64 nearest-neighbour matches with matches propagated through SAE32.

conditions.value: direct SAE16–SAE64 matches versus SAE16–SAE32–SAE64 matches

rows.measure: Set overlap of recovered SAE64 features
rows.value: Overlap is described as roughly bimodal; apart from perfect-overlap triplets, it generally ranges from 0 to 0.6. The vast majority of perfect-overlap sets are at most 3 features.
rows.note: The authors say this supports the finding that features across models with different k are not well-aligned.
rows.check: Authors say clean splitting geometry would give consistent sets. Instead, overlap is bimodal and mostly 0–0.6 outside perfect-overlap triplets, so splitting is not clean or nested. Removed V5.

rows.subject: astro-ph SAE64
rows.operation_detail: Identified novel features in a larger SAE by comparing features to nearest neighbours in smaller SAEs.
rows.measure: Presence of features without related features in smaller SAEs
rows.value: The paper describes novel, more granular features, including Quasi-periodic oscillations in blazars, appearing only in SAE64; it also reports LTB Models and Lyman Break Galaxies as unrelated additional SAE64 features.
rows.note: Supports the novel-feature component of V5; the smaller-to-larger latent-combination component is not tested.
rows.check: Novel SAE64-only features (QPOs in blazars; LTB/LBG). Qualitative examples only.

source_check.notes: Cross-size evidence is qualitative and comes from hand-picked astro-ph examples (Figs. 16–17) plus figure-only distributions (Fig. 9 pools astro-ph and cs.LG). Table 1 caption says medians, while the body text says means. The study steers within-SAE co-activation families in search (Sec. 5.2); these are not cross-size split families.

statements.correction: Fig. 9 (r1, r2): NN decoder cosine falls as k and n rise, with astro-ph and cs.LG pooled. Recurrence is more common at lower k per Sec. 4.1/Fig. 16 and Fig. 18a (>1100 triplets at >0.95 cosine for k=16, dropping sharply as k rises).
statements.problem: Calls r1/r2 'Astro-ph SAEs', but Figure 9 pools astro-ph and cs.LG distributions. The finding that recurrence is more common at lower k does not come from r1/r2.

statements.correction: Fig. 18b: the set overlap between direct SAE16→SAE64 and chained SAE16→SAE32→SAE64 nearest-neighbour matches is roughly bimodal. Apart from perfect-overlap triplets, it generally ranges 0–0.6.
statements.problem: 'Mostly 0–0.6' leaves out the second mode of a bimodal distribution: perfect-overlap triplets sit at 1. Also, the quantity is the overlap between direct and chained match sets, not 'chain overlaps'.

statements.correction: Fig. 17b: LTB Models and LBGs first appear in SAE64, and SAE16/SAE32 learn no related higher-level concept; the authors say the grouping may be a spurious acronym correlation. Fig. 17a: QPOs in blazars appears only in SAE64, as a more granular feature under the periodicity feature present in SAE16/32/64.
statements.problem: Gives QPOs in blazars as a feature with no related feature in SAE16/SAE32. The text presents it as a granular split under the periodicity feature, which is present in all three SAEs. Only LTB/LBG are said to lack related smaller-SAE concepts.

statements.correction: NN decoder cosine falls with k and n: Sec. 4.1, Fig. 9 (r1, r2; astro-ph and cs.LG pooled). Recurrence is higher at lower k: Sec. 4.1, Fig. 18a. Family Ddiag/Doff: Table 1, 0.89–5.87, varying by dataset and (k, n); E.2 activation-similarity ratios are in Fig. 19.
statements.problem: Cites r8, which records novel SAE64 features, not these trends. The NN-similarity trend is in r1/r2, with datasets pooled. In-block activation-similarity ratios also have numbers in Table 1, so they are not figure-only.

reader_labels.reason: The study finds some recurring, semantically related split features, but similarity decreases with increasing k or n, includes unrelated nearest neighbours, and does not establish input partitioning (r1–r7).
